lesson.title: Plotting Points: Turning Numbers into a Physical Mark
lesson.summary: Plotting a point means translating its ordered pair into a physical location on the coordinate plane by moving horizontally for x and then vertically for y.
lesson.body:
An ordered pair on paper is just two numbers until it gets plotted, at which point it becomes an actual location you can see, measure, and connect to other points. Plotting a point is a two-step process that follows directly from what the x-coordinate and y-coordinate each mean. Starting at the origin, first move horizontally according to the x-coordinate: right if it is positive, left if it is negative, and not at all if it is zero. Then, from that new horizontal position, move vertically according to the y-coordinate: up if it is positive, down if it is negative. Mark the spot where you land, and that mark is the plotted point.

The order of operations here is not arbitrary. Because the x-coordinate is listed first in the pair, it is handled first, and the y-coordinate is handled second, exactly matching the order they appear in (x, y). Doing the vertical move before the horizontal move can still land on the correct point, since the two movements are independent of one another, but practicing the standard order, horizontal then vertical, builds a habit that generalizes well once graphs get more complicated and multiple points need to be plotted quickly and accurately.

Here is a worked example. To plot the point (-3, 5), start at the origin (0, 0). Move 3 units to the left, since the x-coordinate is negative 3. From there, move 5 units up, since the y-coordinate is positive 5. Mark that location. Because the x-coordinate is negative and the y-coordinate is positive, this point should land in Quadrant II, and indeed it does, confirming the plotting was done correctly using the sign rules covered in the previous chapter. This kind of quick cross-check, comparing the expected quadrant to the actual plotted location, is a habit worth building early.

A second worked example shows how plotting reveals relationships between points. Plot A at (2, -4) and B at (2, 3). Both points share the x-coordinate 2, so they lie on the same vertical line, directly above and below one another. The vertical distance between them can be found by subtracting their y-coordinates: 3 - (-4) = 7. So A and B sit exactly 7 units apart along that vertical line. This kind of distance measurement, using shared coordinates to line points up, is exactly what later chapters build on when measuring vertical and horizontal change between two points on a line.

Plotting accurately matters because every graph, whether it is a simple scatter of individual points or a full straight line, is built up from this same one-point-at-a-time process. Getting comfortable translating an ordered pair into a physical mark on the plane is the foundation for graphing functions, which is exactly where the next chapters are headed, starting with linear functions and how their outputs behave as ordered pairs.
